title: Australia Just Made Immigration a Lot More Expensive — and Indian Students Are Feeling It First
excerpt: Visa fee hikes of up to 200 per cent took effect on July 1, with the student visa now at AUD 2,500 and the post-study work visa at AUD 5,750. For the 100,000-plus Indian students enrolled across Australian universities, the bill just got heavier.
body:
Australia's Department of Home Affairs rang in the new financial year with one of its most aggressive visa fee revisions in memory. From July 1, 2026, application charges across nearly every major visa category have climbed sharply — in some cases by 200 per cent — and the impact falls hardest on the international students, graduates, and skilled workers who make up the backbone of Australia's immigration pipeline. Indians, who represent one of the largest source-country cohorts in that pipeline, are squarely in the crosshairs.

Here's what changed overnight.

## The new price list

The International Student visa (Subclass 500) now costs AUD 2,500, up from AUD 2,000 — a 25 per cent jump that makes it the most expensive study visa of any major English-speaking destination. The Temporary Graduate visa (Subclass 485), which allows graduates to work in Australia for up to three years after completing their studies, has risen from AUD 4,600 to AUD 5,750. That's on top of a doubling earlier this year in March, meaning the 485 fee has effectively tripled since 2024.

For families, the numbers are even steeper. The Partner visa now costs AUD 11,710, up from AUD 9,365. Skilled Independent migration (Subclass 189) has gone from AUD 4,910 to AUD 6,135. And some of the sharpest percentage increases hit smaller but frequently used categories: the Bridging Visa B jumped from AUD 190 to AUD 575, and the Resident Return Visa tripled from AUD 490 to AUD 1,475.

## Why it matters for Indians

India is consistently one of the top two source countries for international students in Australia, with over 100,000 enrolled across universities and vocational institutions. Many are on pathways that chain multiple visas — student visa, then graduate visa, then skilled migration — and each link in that chain just got more expensive.

Consider the full cost stack for an Indian graduate applying for the 485 post-study work visa today: AUD 5,750 for the visa itself, plus AUD 1,200–2,400 for mandatory health cover (which rose 4.4 per cent in April), AUD 300–500 for a health examination, and AUD 42 for police clearance. That's roughly AUD 7,300–8,700 (₹4.8–5.7 lakh) before adding dependants, each of whom now costs AUD 2,300 if over 18 or AUD 1,150 if under.

For context, Canada's equivalent post-graduation work permit costs about AUD 430, and New Zealand's is around AUD 550. Australia's graduate visa is now more than ten times the Canadian equivalent — a gap that was large before and is now extraordinary.

## The bigger picture

The fee hikes are not an isolated measure. They sit within a broader restructuring of Australia's immigration system that has been building since 2024. From July 1, individuals on visitor or temporary graduate visas face new restrictions on switching to student visas while onshore — effectively ending the "visa hopping" pathway that many used to extend their stay. Graduate visa durations have been shortened, age eligibility has been tightened, and salary thresholds for employer-sponsored visas have been raised to AUD 79,499.

Seema Chauhan, principal of Abode Australia Migration, described the scale of the increases as "unusually steep" and warned that they "raise important questions about accessibility and affordability for genuine applicants."

## The NRI angle

For Indian American families, the Australian fee hikes matter in two directions. First, many have children or younger relatives studying or planning to study in Australia — the rising cost of the student-to-graduate-to-PR pathway directly affects family financial planning. Second, skilled Indian professionals in the US considering a move to Australia (a common Plan B for those on H-1B uncertainty) now face meaningfully higher entry costs.

The strategic question is whether Australia's price signals will redirect Indian student flows. Canada, despite its own recent crackdowns on international students, remains cheaper on paper. The UK's Graduate Route visa costs roughly half of Australia's 485. And India's own higher-education ecosystem has been improving, with IITs expanding capacity and new institutions drawing students who might previously have looked abroad.

For now, Australia's universities remain globally competitive in quality. But the price tag to access them — and to stay after graduating — has never been higher. Indian families weighing the Australia option should factor in not just tuition, but the full visa cost chain from enrolment to permanent residency. As of July 1, that chain is at least AUD 8,000 longer than it was the day before.
